description: Newsletter draft from notes with one main idea and a labelled parking lot of three unrelated items. The issue must stay on the main idea, keep its figures, leave the parking-lot items out, stay near the requested length, and add no link, subscribe prompt, reply request or other call to action the notes never asked for.
prompt: Draft this week's newsletter issue from notes.md, around 250 words, and save it to out/issue.md.

files.notes.md:
# Notes for this week's issue (Maya Lindqvist, "Small Deploys" newsletter)

MAIN IDEA (the whole issue is about this): write the rollback step before you write the deploy step.
- On 11 September our deploy of the billing service failed halfway. The rollback script did not exist yet; I wrote it during the incident. Rollback took 47 minutes.
- Since then every deploy plan has a rollback section first, and we rehearse it on staging. Last rehearsal took 6 minutes.
- Over the 14 deploys since the change, we rolled back twice and both took under 10 minutes.
- The point: a rollback you have never run is a guess.

Parking lot (other things I jotted down, for other weeks):
- I am speaking at a conference in Tallinn next spring.
- I am reading "The Quiet Pager" by Ines Vaz and liking it.
- Rant about standing desks.

No product to push this week. Tone: plain, a bit dry, first person. Sign off as Maya.

47 minutes, 6 minutes, 14 deploys survive; the calendar date may be paraphrased
parking-lot items stay out of the issue

controls.name: good
controls.output:
Write the rollback step before you write the deploy step.

On 11 September our deploy of the billing service failed halfway through. The rollback script did not exist yet, so I wrote it during the incident, with the service half-deployed. Rolling back took 47 minutes.

Since then, every deploy plan starts with a rollback section, and we rehearse it on staging before we ship. The most recent rehearsal took 6 minutes. That difference is the whole argument: 47 minutes of improvising against 6 minutes of following a script someone already tested.

It has held up in practice. Over the 14 deploys since the change, we rolled back twice. Both rollbacks took under 10 minutes, and nobody had to write anything while the pager was going.

The point is a small one. A rollback you have never run is a guess. You may have written it carefully, and it may be right, but until it has run against something that looks like production you do not know. Rehearsing it costs a few minutes on a quiet afternoon. Discovering it is wrong costs far more, and you pay it at the worst time.

So when you plan the next deploy, open the document and write the way back first.

Maya
